hints: Recall what concentration and temperature define the standard state for all aqueous ions in a half cell.
walkthrough:
Picture what standard means**
Think of standard conditions as a fair baseline so every $E^{\ominus}$ value can be compared. For any dissolved species that means fixing its concentration, and for the whole cell that means fixing temperature.

Apply to the tin ion system**
Here both the oxidised and reduced forms are ions in the same solution, so you set both [$\text{Sn}^{2+}$] and [$\text{Sn}^{4+}$] to $1.0\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ at $298\ \text{K}$.

hints: Recall which reference half cell is always paired with the unknown half cell when measuring $E^{\ominus}$, and what its electrode, gas and solution are.
Think about why the $\text{Sn}^{4+}$/$\text{Sn}^{2+}$ half cell cannot use a tin rod, and what inert metal must provide the surface for electron transfer.
Consider how the two solutions are connected electrically without mixing, and how the cell e.m.f. is measured with no current drawn.
walkthrough:
Set up the unknown half cell**
$\text{Sn}^{4+} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Sn}^{2+}$ has no solid metal to act as an electrode. So you place a clean platinum wire, which is inert and just conducts electrons, into a beaker containing a mixture of $\text{Sn}^{2+}$(aq) and $\text{Sn}^{4+}$(aq), both at $1.0\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$.

Set up the reference half cell**
Pair it with the standard hydrogen electrode. That is a second Pt electrode dipping into $1.0\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^{+}$(aq) with hydrogen gas at $1$ atm ($101$ kPa) bubbled over the surface through a glass tube, so $2\text{H}^{+} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_{2}$ is established.

Complete the circuit correctly**
Join the two solutions with a salt bridge, for example filter paper soaked in $\text{KNO}_{3}$(aq), with each end dipping below the liquid level. Join the two Pt electrodes by external wire through a high resistance voltmeter. Label all solutions, gas, electrodes, salt bridge and meter.

Final answer: Left beaker: $\text{Sn}^{2+}$(aq) + $\text{Sn}^{4+}$(aq), both $1.0\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$, with Pt (or C/graphite) electrode. Right beaker: $\text{H}^{+}$(aq) $1.0\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ with Pt electrode and $\text{H}_{2}$(g) at 1 atm bubbled over it via gas inlet. Beakers linked by salt bridge dipping into both solutions, electrodes joined by wire through a voltmeter.

hints: Identify the two reduction half equations that could combine $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ oxidation with $\text{Cl}_{2}$ reduction, and read their $E^{\ominus}$ values from Table 3.1.
Recall how the sign of $E_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{positive} - E^{\ominus}_{negative}$ tells you whether the mixture will react under standard conditions.
walkthrough:
Write what would have to happen**
For $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ to react, $\text{Cl}^{-}$ would have to be oxidised to $\text{Cl}_{2}$ and $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ reduced to $\text{Sn}$. Pull the two reduction equations from the table: $\text{Cl}_{2} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Cl}^{-}$, $E^{\ominus} = +1.36\ \text{V}$ and $\text{Sn}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Sn}$, $E^{\ominus} = -0.14\ \text{V}$.

Check the cell e.m.f.**
The more positive electrode stays as reduction ($\text{Cl}_{2}$/$\text{Cl}^{-}$) and the more negative is reversed. So $$E_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{reduction} - E^{\ominus}_{oxidation} = -0.14 - (+1.36) = -1.50\ \text{V}$$ A negative $E_{cell}$ means the free energy change is positive, so no reaction occurs. $\text{Cl}^{-}$ is too weak a reductant to reduce $\text{Sn}^{2+}$.

Final answer: No reaction. $E^{\ominus}$($\text{Cl}_{2}$/$\text{Cl}^{-}$) = $+1.36\ \text{V}$, $E^{\ominus}$($\text{Sn}^{2+}$/$\text{Sn}$) = $-0.14\ \text{V}$. For $\text{Sn}^{2+} + 2\text{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Sn} + \text{Cl}_{2}$, $E_{cell} = -0.14 - (+1.36) = -1.50\ \text{V} < 0$, so not feasible.

hints: Compare $E^{\ominus}$($\text{Sn}^{4+}$/$\text{Sn}^{2+}$) = $+0.15\ \text{V}$ with the vanadium couples and decide which vanadium species $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ can reduce.
Balance electrons by remembering $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ gives 2 electrons while each $\text{VO}^{2+}$ to $\text{V}^{3+}$ change takes 1 electron, then balance $\text{H}^{+}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the oxidant and reductant**
$E^{\ominus}$($\text{VO}^{2+}$/$\text{V}^{3+}$) = $+0.34\ \text{V}$ is more positive than $E^{\ominus}$($\text{Sn}^{4+}$/$\text{Sn}^{2+}$) = $+0.15\ \text{V}$. That means $\text{VO}^{2+}$ is the stronger oxidant and will be reduced, while $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ is the stronger reductant and will be oxidised. $E_{cell} = +0.34 - 0.15 = +0.19\ \text{V}$, positive so feasible.

Combine and balance**
Write the halves: $$\text{Sn}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} + 2e^{-}$$ $$\text{VO}^{2+} + 2\text{H}^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{V}^{3+} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ Multiply the vanadium half equation by 2 to cancel the 2 electrons from tin, then add: $$\text{Sn}^{2+} + 2\text{VO}^{2+} + 4\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} + 2\text{V}^{3+} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ Check atoms and charge: both sides $+8$ charge, Sn, V, O and H all balance.

hints: Calculate moles of Sn deposited from its mass, then use the fact that the same charge passed means moles of electrons is the same for both cells.
Relate moles of Al to moles of Sn using the electron stoichiometry: $\text{Sn}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Sn}$ versus $\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Al}$.
walkthrough:
Convert tin mass to moles of electrons**
Moles of Sn is mass over molar mass: $$n(\text{Sn}) = \frac{2.95}{118.7} = 0.02485\ \text{mol}$$ Each Sn needs 2 electrons, $\text{Sn}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Sn}$, so moles of electrons passed is $2 \times n(\text{Sn})$. You do not need $Q = It$ because $I$ and $t$ are identical for aluminium.

Scale to aluminium and convert to mass**
Aluminium needs 3 electrons, $\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Al}$. Same electrons means: $$n(\text{Al}) = \frac{2}{3} \times n(\text{Sn}) = \frac{2}{3} \times 0.02485 = 0.01657\ \text{mol}$$ Then $$m(\text{Al}) = n \times M = 0.01657 \times 27.0 = 0.447\ \text{g} \approx 0.448\ \text{g}$$ to three significant figures.
Final answer: moles Sn = $2.95/118.7 = 0.0249\ \text{mol}$; moles Al = $2/3 \times 0.0249 = 0.0166\ \text{mol}$; mass Al = $0.0166 \times 27.0 = 0.448\ \text{g}$ (3 s.f.).
